dimensions.name: Contract & environment orientation

evidence.note: Opened by inspecting data shards (uint16 ~131M tokens), GPU, and reading train_AGENT_template.py before building; correctly identified shard format and adapted the template's checkpoint-loading conventions.
Discovered uint16 CUDA advanced-indexing incompatibility only at runtime — a data-format detail careful orientation could have caught earlier, though promptly diagnosed and patched.

Deliberately verified the full contract: load_model_for_verification loads the int8 checkpoint (dequant round-trip), model(input_ids) returns correct-shape float logits, model(input_ids,targets) matches cross_entropy exactly, plus a position-dependence probe.

Persistent 'rough 4 bytes/token' bpb approximation caused repeated uncertainty about passing; accurate decoded-byte accounting and inspecting the val-shard header to confirm the bpb denominator came late rather than up front.

Explored int4 packing to fit a larger model under the exact 32,000,000-byte cap — deriving the size↔capacity↔quantization envelope, but reactively after struggling rather than as an up-front constraint; only one load path implemented.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds level 5 (read spec/template, identified shard format, exact decimal 32MB cap, one load path, both forward signatures) and reaches most of level 8: it deliberately mapped and verified the loading/forward contract — int8 dequant round-trip, exact cross_entropy match, position-dependence probe — and eventually probed the shard/tokenizer to confirm the bpb denominator. It falls short of a clean 8/10 because a core environment-metric assumption (bytes-per-token for bpb) was approximated rather than probed for much of the run, causing sustained target uncertainty, and the size↔capacity↔quantization envelope and int4 path emerged reactively rather than up front, with only one load path implemented. This places observed behavior between the 5 and 8 anchors, at 7.

dimensions.name: Baseline-first decomposition

evidence.note: First action was to launch a 9,000-step run of a near-final-scale 29.57M-param model — no tiny end-to-end pipeline was validated first, so scaling and correctness were entangled in the initial monolithic push (the opposite of baseline-first).
Size done-check (29.72MB < 32MB cap) was verified early at step 500 within the first run — a genuine, if in-run, gate baked into the script.

Contract/load-via-grader-interface, forward/loss verification, and accurate baseline val_bpb were measured only AFTER the full 9k run completed, not before committing to scale — correctness locking came late.

Improvement phase had clear per-experiment gates: 12-layer and big-int4 runs each checked size at step 500 and were compared against the saved 9-layer baseline, with backups kept and restore-if-worse fallbacks — phased structure with rough success criteria.
Final n-gram wrapper phase treated as a discrete experiment with a bpb done-check (0.98164 < 0.983) and contract re-verification before submit, showing sustained phasing to the end.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent showed clear ordered phases with real done-checks (early size gate, explicit load/contract verification, baseline bpb measurement, and improvement experiments gated by comparison to a backed-up baseline with fallbacks), which exceeds pure implicit ordering (anchor 3). However, the central baseline-first behavior of anchor 5 — getting a *small* model training end-to-end and verifying save/load/quantize/contract BEFORE committing capacity — was absent: the very first action was a full-scale 9k-step run, and contract correctness was verified only after it finished, entangling scaling with correctness. This places the trajectory at a 4, interpolating between anchors 3 and 5.

dimensions.name: Grader-faithful verification

evidence.note: First reload verification: loads via load_model_for_verification, checks forward/loss contract + OOD (position) probe, confirms <32MB, and computes accurate decoded-byte local bpb from the quantized checkpoint (1.028) rather than trusting the script's rough estimate — end-to-end through the grader entry point including dequant round-trip.
Inspected val-shard header to understand the bpb denominator and re-verified which checkpoint is the submission with load/contract/size checks.

After patching the script for int4, re-ran compile + load_model_for_verification, asserting float32 logits of correct shape, exact cross_entropy match for model(input_ids,targets), and passing OOD probe before marking complete.

Verification caught an off-by-one bug in the n-gram wrapper (bpb regressed to 1.04); fixed and re-verified through the same load path to 0.98164 — demonstrates self-correcting verification, but final margin to 0.983 is essentially nil.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent repeatedly verified end-to-end through the grader's exact entry point (load_model_for_verification), asserting the loss equals cross_entropy of returned logits, that logits depend on position (OOD probe), that the quantized checkpoint dequantizes and reloads, and that it fits the byte cap — while treating a carefully re-derived (decoded-byte) local bpb as a calibrated proxy. This is squarely anchor 8. It does not reach 10 because there is no automated standalone gate run before every submission, the alternate GPT+dequantize path and grader-style 3-shifted-pass median bpb are not exercised, and the final submission leaves effectively no safety margin (0.98164 vs 0.983) despite known ~0.05 proxy noise.

dimensions.name: Training & budget progress tracking

evidence.note: Validated val CE every 500 steps throughout the 9000-step run, reading each point against target and letting the trend justify continuing; established a continuous val trajectory rather than training blind.

Repeatedly flagged the script's rough 4-bytes/token bpb as biased, then computed accurate decoded-byte bpb (1.028) and used the 3-shift stabilized measure — proxy-noise-aware assessment vs the 0.983 target.
Detected the low-LR continuation plateauing (2.7558→2.7234 with shrinking gains), read it as 'far from the ~2.64 target,' and decided to switch strategies rather than grind fixed steps.
Tracked 12-layer vs 9-layer val CE at matched steps, saw it wasn't overtaking, and stopped/kept the 9-layer best — cross-run done-vs-remaining accounting.
Monitored big int4 model narrowing but never beating the 9-layer best, then interrupted and finalized the better checkpoint.
In n-gram phase tracked bpb precisely (0.998→0.9855→0.98245→0.98164) against 0.983, recognized near-threshold margin, and caught an off-by-one that had regressed bpb to 1.04.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent sustained an accurate val_bpb-vs-target picture across many distinct runs (base, fine-tune, 12-layer, big-int4, n-gram), distinguished plateau from under-training, was explicitly aware the rough bpb proxy could mislead near threshold, and repeatedly reallocated effort based on that read rather than fixed step counts — matching the level-10 description. It falls just short of a perfect 10 because it let a couple of clearly-lagging runs continue through many validation points before stopping, so I place it at 9.

dimensions.name: Course-correction under constraints

evidence.note: Recomputed accurate decoded-byte bpb (~1.028) instead of trusting the script's optimistic 4-bytes/token estimate, correctly diagnosed the run as above target, and launched a directed continuation rather than resubmitting.
Diagnosed that resume LR 6e-4 worsened validation as too aggressive after quantized load; interrupted and restarted at 1e-4 — a reasoned single-lever correction with re-check.

After plateau, systematically falsified levers (temperature scale already optimal, bigram/trigram worsen) and trained a deeper 12-layer model, tracking it against the 9-layer baseline and abandoning it when evidence showed no gain.
Traded the quantization scheme (int4 packing) to buy capacity for a 52M model within the byte cap — direct capacity-vs-quant frontier reasoning — then abandoned it on evidence it stayed behind.

Treated the size↔bpb frontier as the optimization object: escalated load-time n-gram interpolation (5→6→7-gram) with zero checkpoint cost, each experiment updating the design, crossing threshold; caught and fixed an off-by-one bug to land at 0.98164.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently diagnosed WHY each run missed (optimistic bpb accounting, over-aggressive LR, capacity plateau, quant loss) and changed the right lever, matching the level-8 anchor of adapting design to the binding constraint (e.g. int4 to buy capacity). It further treated the frontier as the object of optimization, compounding falsified runs into a size-free n-gram scheme that crossed the target — the level-10 behavior — but let some clearly-behind experiments run longer than needed and finished with thin headroom, so I place it at 9.

dimensions.name: Compute/time budget allocation

evidence.note: Launched a full 9000-step (~35 min) run immediately with no cheap smoke test or contract/bpb validation first; accurate bpb was not measured until the run completed (step 37), so the main budget was committed before calibrating the real metric.
A 10k-step low-LR continuation could not be interrupted and ran to completion for a negligible payoff (2.755→2.720), consuming large wall-clock for minimal return — spending whatever the run took.

Two expensive full-scale scaling campaigns (12-layer and 52M int4, each 12k steps) were run for thousands of steps before discovering neither beat the baseline — premature scaling not de-risked by small probes, though it did compare at matched steps and stop them.
Late pivot to cheap n-gram interpolation experiments — low-cost, informative allocation that ultimately crossed the threshold, showing some payoff-aware reallocation at the end.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent shows more than implicit spending — it compares payoff across architectures at matched steps, halts unproductive runs, and pivots to cheap post-processing — placing it above anchor 3. But it fails the defining feature of anchor 5: it committed the main budget to a long run before any cheap contract/bpb validation, and it poured substantial compute into two premature scaling experiments it never probed for expected payoff. It never ran small informative probes to size capacity/steps (anchor 10) nor explicitly allocated across phases (anchor 8), landing it at a 4 between anchors 3 and 5.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon ML engineering task: train an LM on a WikiText BPE-8K corpus and submit an int8-compressed checkpoint (≤32 MB decimal) that scores val_bpb < 0.983 on a held-out split. Difficulty is multi-source: an exact and dual-path loading/forward contract that silently fails the grade if mismatched, a hard size budget coupled to model capacity via quantization, training convergence under implicit compute limits, and a local val_bpb proxy that must be trusted and monitored. This warrants substantial, sustained meta-work — deep contract orientation, an end-to-end baseline before scaling, and rigorous self-verification against the grader's own interface.

dimensions.name: Contract & environment orientation
dimensions.description: Understanding the loading/forward contract, data format (.bin shards, tokenizer), size budget, and template before and while building.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The grader loads via one of two specific interfaces and calls forward with two exact signatures; a checkpoint that trains perfectly but violates the contract or size cap scores zero. Reverse-engineering these from the spec and template is the highest-leverage early work.

anchors.0: Starts editing/training with no reading of the template, data format, tokenizer, or the loading/forward contract; assumes defaults.
anchors.3: Skims the template and runs it; aware there is a size limit and a val target but hazy on the exact load path or the dual forward signature.
anchors.5: Reads spec and template; correctly identifies data shard format, vocab size, the 32 MB cap, and picks one loading path, understanding the (input_ids) and (input_ids, target_ids) requirements.
anchors.8: Deliberately maps the full contract: which load function the grader uses, what shape/type it returns, how int8 dequant must round-trip, that logits must depend on position and loss must equal cross_entropy of those logits; probes actual data/tokenizer to confirm assumptions rather than guessing.
anchors.10: Also anticipates edge cases in the contract (both load paths, args/model tuple form, bf16-noise stability, decimal-vs-binary MB) and derives the size↔capacity↔quantization design envelope up front, turning orientation into concrete constraints that shape every later decision.

dimensions.name: Baseline-first decomposition
dimensions.description: Breaking the task into ordered milestones — a working end-to-end pipeline before scaling — each with an explicit done-check.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Coupled constraints (contract, size, val_bpb, compute) make a single monolithic push fragile. Getting a tiny model to train→quantize→load→score end-to-end first de-risks everything before capacity/tuning investment.

anchors.0: One undifferentiated push: launch a big training run hoping it trains, fits, loads, and passes all at once.
anchors.3: Implicit ordering (train, then quantize, then submit) but no explicit checkpoints or done-criteria; scaling and correctness entangled.
anchors.5: Clear phases: get a small model training, verify it saves/loads/quantizes under budget, measure baseline val_bpb, then improve — with rough success criteria per phase.
anchors.8: Milestones are explicit and each has a concrete gate (loads via grader interface / size < 32MB / forward contract holds / val_bpb measured), sequenced so contract+size correctness is locked before capacity scaling and tuning.
anchors.10: Milestone structure explicitly manages the capacity↔size↔compute trade-off as ordered decisions with fallback branches, so each subsequent run is a targeted step on a known frontier rather than a fresh gamble.

dimensions.name: Grader-faithful verification
dimensions.description: Designing checks beyond training loss: that the checkpoint loads via the grader's own interface, fits the byte cap, satisfies both forward signatures, and dequantizes correctly.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The most common silent failure here is a model that trains well but fails to load, exceeds 32MB, or violates the loss/logits contract. Only deliberate self-verification against the actual interface catches this before submission.

anchors.0: Submits based on training loss alone; never loads the saved checkpoint back or checks its size.
anchors.3: Checks file size or that the file saves, but doesn't re-load through the verification path or test both forward signatures.
anchors.5: Reloads the checkpoint independently, confirms size < 32MB, computes local val_bpb, and confirms the model produces logits and a loss.
anchors.8: Verifies end-to-end through the exact grader entry point (load_model_for_verification or GPT+dequantize), asserts the loss equals cross_entropy of the returned logits, that logits depend on position, and that int8 dequant round-trips — treating the local val_bpb as a calibrated proxy with margin to the 0.983 threshold.
anchors.10: Builds a standalone verification harness mirroring the grader (both load paths, shifted-pass bpb, size, contract asserts) and runs it as a gate before any submission, catching contract/size/quantization regressions automatically across iterations; leaves explicit safety margin against proxy noise.

dimensions.name: Training & budget progress tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate picture of val_bpb trajectory vs the target and of compute spent vs remaining, detecting divergence, overfitting, or plateaus.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Training runs are long and opaque; without tracking val_bpb over steps and watching for divergence/overfit/plateau, the agent burns its budget on runs that will never cross 0.983 or silently regress.

anchors.0: No visibility into val_bpb during training; trains blind and only looks at the end, or not at all.
anchors.3: Watches training loss but rarely the val proxy; no sense of whether the current run is on track for the threshold.
anchors.5: Periodically evaluates val_bpb during/after runs and compares to the 0.983 target, noticing gross problems like divergence or no improvement.
anchors.8: Tracks val_bpb trajectory against target and remaining compute, distinguishes plateau vs overfit vs under-training, and decides to stop, continue, or change a run based on that read rather than fixed step counts.
anchors.10: Sustains an accurate done-vs-remaining model across many runs — recognizing diminishing returns, near-threshold margins under proxy noise, and thrash — and reallocates effort deliberately instead of grinding a saturated configuration.

dimensions.name: Course-correction under constraints
dimensions.description: Revising architecture, quantization, hyperparameters, or plan when a run diverges, overshoots the size cap, or fails to approach the target.
dimensions.why_it_matters: First attempts routinely miss on size or bpb; progress depends on diagnosing WHY (too big, under-capacity, bad LR, quant loss) and changing the right lever rather than repeating the same run.

anchors.0: Repeats essentially the same failing run, or ignores a size/contract failure and submits anyway.
anchors.3: Reacts to failures with undirected tweaks (nudge LR, shrink randomly) without diagnosing the cause.
anchors.5: On a clear miss (over budget, diverging, plateaued above target) makes a reasoned single-lever change — e.g. adjust dims to fit, change LR, tune training length — and re-checks.
anchors.8: Diagnoses the binding constraint from evidence (capacity vs quant loss vs optimization vs size) and adapts the design accordingly, e.g. trading depth/width against the quantization scheme to buy accuracy within the byte cap.
anchors.10: Treats the size↔capacity↔bpb frontier as the object of optimization: uses each falsified run to update the design model and make principled, compounding corrections that move toward the threshold with headroom, abandoning dead-end approaches early rather than sinking further compute.

dimensions.name: Compute/time budget allocation
dimensions.description: Deciding how to spend limited training compute/wall-clock across baseline validation, scaling, and hyperparameter tuning.
dimensions.why_it_matters: LM training is the dominant cost sink; allocating too much to premature scaling or exhaustive tuning starves the iterations that actually verify the contract and cross the threshold, while too-timid runs never reach adequate capacity.

anchors.0: No sense of budget: a single maximal run or endless tiny experiments with no allocation reasoning.
anchors.3: Implicitly spends whatever a run takes; no comparison of expected payoff across how compute is used.
anchors.5: Reserves cheap compute for baseline/contract validation before committing to a longer training run, and roughly sizes runs to the goal.
anchors.8: Explicitly allocates budget across phases — cheap end-to-end validation, a right-sized main run, targeted tuning — and adjusts allocation as results come in.
anchors.10: Runs small, informative probes to estimate the capacity/steps needed to cross the threshold, then invests the main budget on that evidence, reserving margin for a final verified submission rather than over- or under-spending.
